title: Should Jude Bellingham’s first goal for England have stood? Norway don’t think so
text:
FIFA World

Cup 2026

Norway believed the ball hit the overhead sky cam before Bellingham went on to score England's first-half equaliser Fox Sports

Norway were left fuming after they believed the ball hit the sky cam above the pitch and directly led to England’s equalising goal during the World Cup quarter-final at Hard Rock Stadium.

According to footage from U.S. host broadcaster Fox, goalkeeper Orjan Nyland’s goal kick appeared to hit the camera that is suspended on wires above the field during Saturday’s quarter-final in Miami.

Advertisement

The apparent intervention caused a change of possession, with the ball then falling to England midfielder Elliot Anderson. Anderson passed the ball on to Anthony Gordon, who in turn fed Jude Bellingham to score and make it 1-1.

The equalising goal came in first-half stoppage time, with Norway coach Stale Solbakken visibly annoyed with referee Clement Turpin at the half-time interval. Nyland also pointed upwards towards the camera in protest, as did Erling Haaland.

“Just before the goal, the ball hits the cable with the camera on it, causing it to change direction and fall shorter than it should have,” Norway assistant coach Kent Bergersen told TV2 at half-time. “The referee should have spotted that.

“There’s nothing we can do about it now. We’ll just have to grit our teeth and get on with it.”

On the play that led to England's equalizer, the ball hit the FIFA sky cam before the goal. pic.twitter.com/QZgYSVcSpK

— FOX Sports (@FOXSports) July 11, 2026

Despite the protestations, a FIFA official has told The Athletic that the ball chip technology — used in every game of the tournament in the United States, Canada and Mexico — did not indicate that the ball touched anything in mid-air and, according to their data, there was no peak on the sensor.

FIFA later reiterated this with a post on social media. FIFA sources with knowledge of the situation said that there are 16 antennas tracking the signal in HardRock Stadium, which are mounted under the roof and were active as the ball travelled through the air. They added that the footage from the spy cam of the goal was broadcast, and does not shake while showing that footage, indicating it was not struck.

Before England’s goal in minute 45+2 against Norway, the sensor in the Connected Ball showed no peak in the 'heartbeat of the ball' when in the air, and therefore no evidence that the ball touched the overhead wire and changed the movement of the ball. pic.twitter.com/gYf9ukfveT

— FIFA Media (@fifamedia) July 11, 2026

Asked about the incident after the game, Solbakken said: “Well he (the referee) said that he didn’t see it himself and they he didn’t get any message that it actually happened and that’s a good explanation and since FIFA says there was no touch, no signal from chip in ball then he can’t do anything about it. But the ball fell straight down, just in front of the bench … so it did touch it!”

Advertisement

“I was not one of them but (the assistant coach) saw it,” he added. “There has been nothing in the chip, what can I say against that? But the ball drops down straight from heaven! I was looking another way so I wondered what happened. So pretty clear that it hit it, it was a strange thing.”

Andreas Schjelderup had given Norway the lead in the 36th minute, before Bellingham’s equaliser. After it finished 1-1 after 90 minutes — and Norway had seen a goal ruled out for a Haaland push in the 55th minute — Bellingham then scored England’s winning goal in the third minute of extra time.

“It’s the little moments that make the difference in the World Cup,” Haaland told TV 2, when asked about two refereeing decisions potentially going against Norway. “Against Brazil, we managed to tip the balance in our favour. Today, we had a 50/50 call go against us. That makes it difficult. England are a good side.”

The “outside interference” section of the International Football Association Board (IFAB) Laws of the Game indicates that if an “other object” enters the field of play during the match, the referee must:

In this case, if Turpin observed the ball hitting the cable, he should have stopped the play when the ball hit the other object — i.e. the sky cam — and restarted the game with a dropped ball.

A dropped ball sees the ball “dropped at its position when play was stopped, unless it hit a match official or outside agent, in which case it is dropped at the position of the interference/contact.”

The Video Assistant Referee is able to intervene if there is clear and obvious evidence that one of the teams suffered an obvious disadvantage. VAR Jerome Brisard clearly did not feel the incident constituted a clear and obvious error and did not intervene.

Adidas manufactures the balls used in World Cups and since Qatar 2022, a 500Hz inertial measurement unit (IMU) motion sensor has been embedded to track data and enhance the VAR system.

Advertisement

The ‘Connected Ball Technology’ (CBT), as Adidas calls it, is combined with player position data and, through artificial intelligence, they offer real-time information to streamline the semi-automated offside process. By delivering data 500 times a second, the sensor helps make the precise moment a ball was touched clear.

Analysis by former Premier League referee Graham Scott

Strictly speaking, you can make a case for outside interference, which means there should be a dropped ball.

But in practice, there has to be some evidence of impact. You would allow play to continue if the ball hit a paper cup or small piece of debris on the pitch if it made no difference to the play. It’s hard to be sure here, but in any event, I think it’s unlikely the VAR would even consider checking a camera angle up in the gods when reviewing the attacking phase.

He would have been focusing on the actions of the players in the build-up, and there was no obvious reason to dig so deep, especially given the pressure on all video officials not to be too forensic, nor to delay the game in an apparent quest to find something wrong with what appears to be a perfectly valid goal.

Alfie Haaland, the father of Erling, posted on social media to congratulate Bellingham after his match-winning display but also hinted at the controversy.

“Well done Bellingham and referee,” he wrote, in reply to a post on Bellingham’s performance at the tournament so far.

“I didn’t see it myself, but we certainly didn’t have any room for error. You might need that in matches like this. It’s a shame,” Norway captain Martin Odegaard told TV 2.

England head coach Thomas Tuchel also said he had not seen the incident: “There is a chip in the ball I am not aware of it, I didn’t see it.”

Asked what was said in the dressing room about the incident, Norway midfielder Sander Berge said: “Just that the ball hit the wire. But it is what it is, and you can’t do much about it after.

Advertisement

“We are feeling more done by 2-1, but again, fine. Tough to take, and it was a tight, close game. They came out on top and we pushed them to the end and did everything.”

“I saw from the bench it looked really strange, so, yeah, I don’t know,” Norway midfielder Morten Thorsby said. “I saw something coming out that there was nothing confirmed, but yeah, the ball, how it went, was really strange from the bench, that’s all I can say. It happened and we have to move on.”

Former referee Christina Unkel suggested a second angle — from the sideline — appears to show the ball not deviating in the air.

“I would post video I have access to that is clean but FIFA will take down for IP infraction,” she posted on X. “Best angle is touchline angle from technical bench showing uninterrupted rainbow arch. Always consider all evidence but what we have access to shows no change of direction or trajectory.”
